source.title: The Triangle of Everything
source.note: Illustrated poster built on the Lineweaver & Patel 'All objects' mass-size diagram.

physics.conventions: W = full width (diameter) in metres, M = mass in kg, both log10. Density lines treat an object as a sphere of diameter W: M = rho (pi/6) W^3.

horizons.name: Hubble radius
horizons.definition: c / H0: the distance at which cosmic expansion carries galaxies away from us at exactly the speed of light today.
horizons.description: A sphere this size, filled at the universe's average density, is exactly its own Schwarzschild size - which is why it sits at the triangle's top corner. It grows over time and will level off at about 1.2x today's size as dark energy takes over.

horizons.name: Edge of the observable universe (particle horizon)
horizons.definition: The farthest distance from which light emitted since the Big Bang has had time to reach us, measured as where that source is today (comoving distance).
horizons.description: It is about 3x the Hubble radius. Light that set out from just beyond the Hubble sphere still reached us, because the Hubble sphere grew and overtook it, and space kept stretching while the light travelled. So galaxies between the two lines are visible even though they recede faster than light today. Nothing beyond this line has ever been able to send us a signal.

macro_dark_matter.source: Jacobs, Starkman & Lynn (2015), 'Macro Dark Matter', MNRAS 450, 3418 (arXiv:1410.2236): unconstrained for nuclear-dense objects of 55 g-1e17 g and 2e20 g-4e24 g (the lower window closes if macros destabilise ordinary matter).

coordinate_systems.norm: px divided by image width/height (0-1) - use for responsive overlays.
coordinate_systems.chart: Values implied by where something is drawn (from the axis calibrations).
coordinate_systems.reference: Standard real-world values compiled for this dataset (not read from the image).
coordinate_systems.log10_density_proxy_kg_m3: log10(mass) - 3*log10(width), the quantity the diagonal density grid tracks.
coordinate_systems.position_is_schematic: True for icons arranged beside the main sequence for legibility; their x position is not a width.

width.note: Bottom axis 'WIDTH 10^n m'. Printed labels -33..24 sit on these ticks and are correct.

mass.note: Right axis 'MASS 10^n kg'. Tick values verified by the solar-mass, tonne and kg reference lines; several printed labels above 0 are wrong (see errata).

energy.note: Left axis 'ENERGY 10^n eV' (also used as temperature). It is the mass axis shifted by ~35.4 decades (E = mc^2; the exact shift is 35.75).

axes.density: See cosmic_timeline.json -> density_ruler (density lines are diagonals of slope 3).

boundaries.meaning: Objects cannot be smaller than their own black-hole size; the upper-left edge of the triangle.
boundaries.equation: log10 M[kg] = log10 W[m] + 26.527217  (W = Schwarzschild diameter 4GM/c^2)
boundaries.chart_fit: log10 M = log10 W + 26.6 (apex to observable universe)
boundaries.extends_beyond: Continues up-right past the observable universe as the edge of the lighter 'future' band.

boundaries.meaning: Quantum uncertainty forbids localising a mass in less than its Compton wavelength; lower-left edge.
boundaries.equation: log10 M[kg] = -log10 W[m] -42.453744  (W = reduced Compton wavelength hbar/Mc)

boundaries.meaning: Nothing larger than the observable universe can be seen; the vertical right edge.
boundaries.equation: log10 W[m] = 26.436883 (diameter of today's Hubble sphere, 2c/H0). The poster draws it at ~25.97.

boundaries.meaning: Horizontal red dotted line through the apex and the grain of salt.
Vertical red dotted line through the apex.
Horizontal dotted line on the energy axis meeting the apex.
Blue dotted line of constant (~water/atomic) density that the everyday objects, planets and stars follow.
boundaries.equation: log10 M[kg] ~= 3 log10 W[m] + 3.7 (chart); water: 3 log10 W + 3.0 (cube) or + 2.72 (sphere)

boundaries.meaning: Red dotted density line from the top ruler to the bottom corner labelled HEAT DEATH OF THE UNIVERSE.
Where the Schwarzschild and Compton limits meet: the Planck mass at the Planck length.

reference.note: Exact crossing of the two walls: half the Planck mass at twice the Planck length (with W = 4GM/c^2 and W = hbar/Mc).

first_appeared.label: 10^-24 seconds after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Hypothetical. A primordial black hole forms with about the mass inside the horizon, M ~ c^3 t / G, so the band grows along the wall as time passes.

regions.note: Hypothetical; formed in the early universe. Lighter than ~5e11 kg they would have evaporated by now; the range shown stops where stellar black holes begin. Chart range = bracket ends projected onto the Schwarzschild line.

first_appeared.label: 200 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: The earliest massive stars collapsed ~200 million years after the Big Bang.

regions.note: Formed by collapse of massive stars (~3 to ~150 solar masses). Chart range = bracket ends projected onto the Schwarzschild line.

first_appeared.label: 700 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Quasars powered by billion-solar-mass black holes existed by ~700 million years.

regions.note: Found at galaxy centres (~1e5 to ~1e11 solar masses). Chart range = bracket ends projected onto the Schwarzschild line.
Speckled area with dashed borders; the gap between the two boxes is drawn as excluded.
Speckled area with dashed borders; the gap between the two boxes is drawn as excluded.
Warm-coloured glow next to the Big Bang apex; the image gives no hard edge. Physically: matter hotter than ~150 MeV (first ~10 µs after the Big Bang).
Labels run along the Compton limit below the particles; they are spaced for legibility, not at their true wavelengths. A rainbow ribbon runs from the particles toward the radio end.

first_appeared.label: 10^-12 seconds after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Light as we know it separated from the weak force at the electroweak transition.

energy.label: ELECTROWEAK
energy.note: Span between the GUT scale and electroweak symmetry breaking (~100 GeV).

energy.label: FUNDAMENTAL PARTICLES
energy.note: Electron (0.511 MeV) to top quark (173 GeV); neutrinos are lighter.

energy.label: 100 °C
energy.note: Drawn ~0.6 decade higher than kT for 373 K so the bracket is legible.

energy.label: BOSE-EINSTEIN CONDENSATE
energy.note: Lab BECs form at ~100 nK-1 µK; drawn ~2 decades lower.
